sections.title: How does the Moneyline odds calculator work?
sections.html:
The Moneyline odds calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports chances against success in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you type in number of consecutive wins, the probability of losing, number of consecutive losses and the stake.

The arithmetic runs locally each time an input changes. The page knows which values you have given it and which it still has to derive, so the results panel is never stale.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Moneyline odds calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Chances against success=-chances for success + chances for success ÷ probability of winning
Chances against success=-probability of losing × chances for success ÷ (probability of losing − 1)
Probability of winning=1 − probability of losing
Decimal odds=((chances against success + chances for success) ÷ chances for success)
American (moneyline odds)=(100 × ((chances against success + chances for success) ÷ chances for success) − 100)
American (moneyline odds)=(-100 ÷ (((chances against success + chances for success) ÷ chances for success) − 1))

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Suppose Chances for success = 10, Probability of winning = 10 %, Number of consecutive wins = 2 and Number of consecutive losses = 2. Working through the relationship above gives Chances against success = 90, American (moneyline odds) = 900, Probability of winning times in a row = 1 % and Probability of losing = 90 %.

Read it as a template. Every number above can be replaced with one of yours; only the relationship between them is fixed.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Chances against success = 90, American (moneyline odds) = 900, Probability of winning times in a row = 1 % and Probability of losing = 90 % should be roughly the size you expected from Chances for success = 10 and Probability of winning = 10 %.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

  • %, opening in percent
  • %, opening in percent

  • Currency, opening in US Dollar

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Moneyline odds calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Checking a result a piece of software produced
  • Deciding how much confidence a sample really supports
  • Turning raw numbers into something you can quote
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — number of consecutive wins, the probability of losing and number of consecutive losses — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Moneyline odds calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns chances against success, derived from number of consecutive wins, the probability of losing and number of consecutive losses. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Moneyline odds calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for number of consecutive wins, the probability of losing, number of consecutive losses and the stake, which is 4 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter probability of winning in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Probability of winning opens in percent and the chip beside it offers 6 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Chances against success = 90. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Moneyline odds calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
